newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli battle over Eisenberg fortune heats up.
newsitem.headline: Israeli battle over Eisenberg fortune heats up.

text.p: A family feud in Israel over a $1 billion fortune intensified on Sunday after the son of late tycoon Shoul Eisenberg questioned the objectivity of court-appointed temporary administrators of the estate.
A Tel Aviv District Court judge, responding to counter-claims by the administrators, said he would try to reach a compromise on the matter by Wednesday, Israel Radio reported.

The Tel Aviv-based Eisenberg, who died of a heart attack in Beijing in March, left behind an empire that spans across Asia, Europe and South America. His family have been disputing the will in Israel's biggest-ever inheritance battle.

The main vehicle for the Eisenberg Group's Israeli investments is the Israel Corp, one of the country's major holding companies with investments in more than 80 firms. It controls Israel's biggest chemicals group, Israel Chemicals Ltd.

In documents filed in Tel Aviv District Court, Eisenberg's son Erwin and son-in-law Yigal Diamant said the temporary administrators of the assets -- two court-appointed lawyers -- had caused tremendous damage to the companies of the estate.
Eisenberg and Diamant alleged, among other things, that the administrators had requested banks to freeze payments by various Eisenberg companies.

Eisenberg said he was close to losing faith in the administrators. He said in the documents filed with the court that he reserved the right to ask the courts to fire them, if he lost faith in their ability to fulfil their obligation to preserve the estate.
Erwin Eisenberg was named chairman of Israel Chemicals and Israel Corp in April.

At the heart of the dispute is a will dating from 1986, in which Eisenberg left 80 percent of his estate to Erwin, his only son, and another five percent to son-in-law Diamant, chief executive of Israel Chemicals.
The remaining 15 percent was divided among three of his four living daughters. His wife Leah received $2 million and her homes while a fourth daughter got nothing.
Leah Eisenberg and her daughters claim that the will is not valid because the document has not been found and only a copy remains. They claim the billionaire died intestate.
Eisenberg's attorneys also filed a motion to expedite the hearings of three witnesses to the 1986 will during the court's summer break.

Shoul Eisenberg established the Eisenberg Group of Companies more than 50 years ago. It is involved in international projects in the areas of iron and steel, electricity generation, utilities, cement, edible oils, chemicals, textiles, shipbuilding, agriculture and water management.
